prompt:
Fill each unshaded cell of the grid with a number that is either 1, 3, or 5. For each cell, exactly one of the touching cells must contain the same number. Here touching includes cells that only share a point, i.e. touch diagonally.

The grid is shown in the picture; below, shaded cells are drawn as $\blacksquare$:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline 1 & \phantom{0} & 1 & \phantom{0} & 3 & \phantom{0} & 5\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & 1 & 1 & 3 & 5 & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare\\\hline \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline 5 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 5 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline\end{array}$$

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the conditions of the problem.

solutions.title: Pairs of equal numbers
solutions.body:
The rule says that the cells with the same number come in **touching pairs**: every cell has exactly one touching cell with its own number, so equal numbers form "dominoes" (possibly diagonal) that do not touch any other cell with that number.

Number rows $1$–$7$ from the top and columns $1$–$7$ from the left.

* The given $1, 1$ in row 4 (columns 3, 4) touch each other, so they are a complete pair: **no other cell touching them can be a 1**. This rules out 1 in row 3, columns 2, 3, 5 in row 5, columns 2–4, and in row 4, column 2.
* The cells in row 2, column 2 and row 1, column 2 touch both given 1's of row 2, so they cannot be 1 (they would see two 1's). Hence the 1 in row 2, column 1 must pair with row 1, column 1 or row 3, column 1, and the 1 in row 2, column 3 with row 1, column 3 or 4, or row 2, column 4.
* Similarly the given $3$ and $5$ in rows 2 and 4 each need exactly one partner, and the two $5$'s in row 7 each need one; a cell that touches two equal given numbers can never take that number.

Repeating these partner arguments (every cell has at most 8 neighbours, and each completed pair removes options from all cells around it) leads to
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 5 & 3 & 3 & 5 & 5 & 3 & 5\\\hline 1 & 5 & 1 & 1 & 3 & 1 & 5\\\hline 1 & 3 & 3 & \blacksquare & 5 & 1 & 3\\\hline \blacksquare & 5 & 1 & 1 & 3 & 5 & 3\\\hline 3 & 3 & 5 & 3 & \blacksquare & 1 & \blacksquare\\\hline 5 & \blacksquare & 1 & 1 & 5 & 1 & 5\\\hline 5 & 3 & 3 & 5 & 3 & 3 & 5\\\hline\end{array}$$

**Check.** Each of the 44 unshaded cells has exactly one touching cell (including diagonals) with the same number; for example the top-left $5$ has neighbours $3$, $1$, $5$ — exactly one 5. A computer search over all fillings confirms the solution is unique.

**Answer: the grid above.**

prompt:
Suppose that the 101 positive integers
$$2024,\ 2025,\ 2026,\ \dots,\ 2124$$
are concatenated in some order to form a 404-digit number. Can this number be prime?
answer: **No.** Since $10^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{9999}$, the number is $\equiv 2024 + 2025 + \dots + 2124 = 101\cdot 2074 \pmod{9999}$, and $101 \mid 9999$, so the number is a multiple of $101$.

solutions.title: Work modulo 101
solutions.body:
Each of the numbers has 4 digits, so the concatenation is
$$N = a_{100}\cdot 10^{400} + a_{99}\cdot 10^{396} + \dots + a_1\cdot 10^4 + a_0,$$
where $a_0, \dots, a_{100}$ is some ordering of $2024, \dots, 2124$.

Since $10^2 = 100 \equiv -1 \pmod{101}$, we have $10^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{101}$, and therefore
$$N \equiv a_{100} + a_{99} + \dots + a_0 = 2024 + 2025 + \dots + 2124 \pmod{101}.$$
This sum has 101 terms with average $\frac{2024 + 2124}{2} = 2074$, so it equals $101\cdot 2074$, a multiple of 101. (Equivalently, work modulo $9999 = 99\cdot 101$, where $10^4 \equiv 1$ as well.)

Hence $101 \mid N$ for every ordering, and since $N > 101$, $N$ is never prime.

**Answer: No.** ∎

prompt: Let $n \ge 2$ be a positive integer, and suppose buildings of height $1, 2, \dots, n$ are built in a row on a street. Two distinct buildings are said to be *roof-friendly* if every building between the two is shorter than both buildings in the pair. For example, if the buildings are arranged $5, 3, 6, 2, 1, 4$, there are 8 roof-friendly pairs: $(5, 3)$, $(5, 6)$, $(3, 6)$, $(6, 2)$, $(6, 4)$, $(2, 1)$, $(2, 4)$, $(1, 4)$. Find, with proof, the minimum and maximum possible number of roof-friendly pairs of buildings, in terms of $n$.

solutions.title: Charge each pair to its shorter building
solutions.body:
**Minimum.** Any two neighbouring buildings are roof-friendly (nothing is between them), so there are always at least $n - 1$ pairs. In the arrangement $1, 2, \dots, n$, a non-adjacent pair $(i, j)$ with $i < j$ has building $i + 1 > i$ between them, so it is not roof-friendly: exactly $n - 1$ pairs.

**Maximum: at most $2n - 3$.** Take a roof-friendly pair and let $u$ be its shorter building and $v$ the taller one, say $v$ is to the right of $u$. All buildings between them are shorter than $u$, and $v$ is taller than $u$, so **$v$ is the first building to the right of $u$ that is taller than $u$**. Hence each building $u$ is the shorter member of at most two roof-friendly pairs: one with the first taller building on its left and one with the first taller building on its right.

* The tallest building ($n$) is never the shorter member: 0 pairs.
* Building $n - 1$ has only one taller building, so it is the shorter member of at most 1 pair.
* Every other building: at most 2 pairs.

So the number of pairs is at most $2(n - 2) + 1 = 2n - 3$.

**Maximum is attained.** In the arrangement $n, 1, 2, \dots, n - 1$, each building $u \le n - 2$ pairs with $u + 1$ (its right neighbour) and with $n$ (everything between them is smaller than $u$), and building $n - 1$ pairs with $n$. That is $2(n-2) + 1 = 2n - 3$ pairs.

(A computer count over all permutations for $n \le 8$ gives minimum $n - 1$ and maximum $2n - 3$.)

**Answer: minimum $n - 1$, maximum $2n - 3$.** ∎

solutions.title: Induction on the tallest building (official idea)
solutions.body:
One can also prove the stronger statement that $2n - 3$ pairs occur exactly when the two tallest buildings stand at the two ends, by induction on $n$ ($n = 2$ is clear).

If the tallest building is in position $k$ with $1 < k < n$, no roof-friendly pair has its members on opposite sides of it, so by induction there are at most $(2k - 3) + (2(n - k + 1) - 3) = 2n - 4$ pairs. If the tallest is at an end but the second tallest is in an interior position $k$, again no pair has its members on opposite sides of position $k$ (the building there is taller than every building except the tallest one at the end, which is itself at the end), so splitting there gives at most $2n - 4$. If the two tallest occupy both ends, split at the third tallest building in position $k$: the left part ($k$ buildings) and right part ($n - k + 1$ buildings) both have their two tallest at their ends, giving exactly $(2k - 3) + (2(n-k+1) - 3)$ pairs, plus the pair of the two tallest buildings: $2n - 3$ in total.

**Answer: minimum $n - 1$, maximum $2n - 3$.** ∎

prompt:
Prove that, for any real numbers $1 \le \sqrt{x} \le y \le x^2$, the following system of equations has a real solution $(a, b, c)$:
$$\begin{aligned} a + b + c &= \frac{x + x^2 + x^4 + y + y^2 + y^4}{2},\\ ab + ac + bc &= \frac{x^3 + x^5 + x^6 + y^3 + y^5 + y^6}{2},\\ abc &= \frac{x^7 + y^7}{2}. \end{aligned}$$
answer: Proof: $(a, b, c)$ are the roots of $P(z) = \frac{Q(z) + R(z)}{2}$ with $Q(z) = (z - x)(z - x^2)(z - x^4)$, $R(z) = (z - y)(z - y^2)(z - y^4)$. With $x \le y$, the sign changes of $P$ at $x, y, x^2, y^2, x^4, y^4$ give three real roots (degenerate cases $y = x$, $y = x^2$ directly).

solutions.title: Vieta and the intermediate value theorem
solutions.body:
**Reformulation.** Let
$$Q(z) = (z - x)(z - x^2)(z - x^4), \qquad R(z) = (z - y)(z - y^2)(z - y^4).$$
Expanding, $Q(z) = z^3 - (x + x^2 + x^4)z^2 + (x^3 + x^5 + x^6)z - x^7$, and similarly for $R$. So the monic cubic $P(z) = \frac{Q(z) + R(z)}{2}$ has coefficients exactly matching the right-hand sides, and by Vieta's formulas, the system has a real solution if and only if $P$ has three real roots (counted with multiplicity); then $(a, b, c)$ are those roots.

**Symmetry.** The condition $\sqrt x \le y \le x^2$ (with $x, y \ge 1$) is equivalent to $\sqrt y \le x \le y^2$, and the system is symmetric in $x, y$. So we may assume $x \le y$. Then $y \le x^2$ gives $y^2 \le x^4$, and we have
$$1 \le x \le y \le x^2 \le y^2 \le x^4 \le y^4.$$

**Main case: $x < y < x^2$** (so all six numbers are distinct and $x > 1$). Evaluating:
* $Q(x) = Q(x^2) = Q(x^4) = 0$, $Q(y) > 0$, $Q(y^2) < 0$, $Q(y^4) > 0$;
* $R(y) = R(y^2) = R(y^4) = 0$, $R(x) < 0$, $R(x^2) > 0$, $R(x^4) < 0$.

(For instance $R(x^2) = (x^2 - y)(x^2 - y^2)(x^2 - y^4)$ has signs $(+)(-)(-)$.) Therefore
$$P(x) < 0 < P(y), \qquad P(x^2) > 0 > P(y^2), \qquad P(x^4) < 0 < P(y^4),$$
and by the intermediate value theorem $P$ has a root in each of the disjoint intervals $(x, y)$, $(x^2, y^2)$, $(x^4, y^4)$: three real roots.

**Case $y = x$:** $P = Q$ has the real roots $x, x^2, x^4$. (This includes $x = 1$, where the condition forces $y = 1$ and $(a, b, c) = (1, 1, 1)$.)

**Case $y = x^2$:** then $R(z) = (z - x^2)(z - x^4)(z - x^8)$, so $P(x^2) = P(x^4) = 0$, and
$$P(z) = \frac{(z - x^2)(z - x^4)\big((z - x) + (z - x^8)\big)}{2} = \frac{(z - x^2)(z - x^4)(2z - x - x^8)}{2},$$
whose third root $\frac{x + x^8}{2}$ is real.

In all cases $P$ has three real roots, which give the required solution $(a, b, c)$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A_1A_2A_3\cdots A_{13}$ be a regular 13-gon, and let lines $A_6A_7$ and $A_8A_9$ intersect at $B$. Show that the shaded area shown is half the area of the entire polygon (including triangle $A_7A_8B$).

In the picture, the vertices are labelled counterclockwise with $A_1$ at the top, so the chords $A_2A_{13}, A_3A_{12}, A_4A_{11}, A_5A_{10}, A_6A_9, A_7A_8$ are horizontal. The shaded regions are the trapezoids $A_2A_3A_{12}A_{13}$, $A_4A_5A_{10}A_{11}$ and $A_6A_7A_8A_9$; triangle $A_7A_8B$ hangs below the 13-gon.
answer: Proof: cancel three pairs of congruent triangles, reduce every remaining triangle to one with base $A_7A_8$ (height measured along the symmetry axis), and use two rhombi on the axis to show the heights balance: $2MD + MA_1 = 2MF + MC$.

solutions.title: Triangles on a common base
solutions.body:
Let $\theta = \frac{180^\circ}{13}$, $s = A_7A_8$, and let $\ell$ be the symmetry axis through $A_1$ and the midpoint $M$ of $A_7A_8$ (it also passes through $B$). An inscribed angle standing on an arc of $k$ sides of the 13-gon equals $k\theta$.

**Step 1: triangulate and cancel.** Split each region by a diagonal:
* shaded: $A_2A_3A_{12}A_{13} = \triangle A_2A_3A_{13} + \triangle A_3A_{12}A_{13}$, $\;A_4A_5A_{10}A_{11} = \triangle A_4A_5A_{11} + \triangle A_5A_{10}A_{11}$, $\;A_6A_7A_8A_9 = \triangle A_6A_7A_9 + \triangle A_7A_8A_9$;
* unshaded: $\triangle A_1A_2A_{13}$, $\;A_3A_4A_{11}A_{12} = \triangle A_3A_4A_{12} + \triangle A_4A_{11}A_{12}$, $\;A_5A_6A_9A_{10} = \triangle A_5A_6A_{10} + \triangle A_6A_9A_{10}$, and $\triangle A_7A_8B$.

Triangles of a regular polygon are congruent when their vertices cut the circle into arcs of the same numbers of sides. So $\triangle A_1A_2A_{13} \cong \triangle A_7A_8A_9$ (arcs $1, 1, 11$), $\triangle A_3A_{12}A_{13} \cong \triangle A_6A_9A_{10}$ (arcs $1, 3, 9$), $\triangle A_4A_{11}A_{12} \cong \triangle A_5A_{10}A_{11}$ (arcs $1, 5, 7$). These cancel, and it remains to show
$$[A_2A_3A_{13}] + [A_4A_5A_{11}] + [A_6A_7A_9] = [A_3A_4A_{12}] + [A_5A_6A_{10}] + [A_7A_8B].$$

**Step 2: move everything onto the base $A_7A_8$.** Let $D$, $F$ be the midpoints of $A_5A_{10}$, $A_3A_{12}$ (on $\ell$).
* $\triangle A_2A_3A_{13} \cong \triangle A_6A_7A_9 \cong \triangle A_7A_8A_5$ (arcs $1, 2, 10$). Since $A_5A_{10} \parallel A_7A_8$, $[A_7A_8A_5] = [A_7A_8D] = \frac12 s\cdot MD$.
* $\triangle A_3A_4A_{12} \cong \triangle A_5A_6A_{10} \cong \triangle A_7A_8A_3$ (arcs $1, 4, 8$), with area $\frac12 s\cdot MF$.
* $\triangle A_4A_5A_{11} \cong \triangle A_7A_8A_1$ (arcs $1, 6, 6$), with area $\frac12 s\cdot MA_1$.
* Let $C = A_5A_8 \cap A_7A_{10}$ (on $\ell$). The exterior angle gives $\angle BA_7A_8 = \angle BA_8A_7 = 180^\circ - 11\theta = 2\theta$, while $\angle A_5A_8A_7 = \angle A_{10}A_7A_8 = 2\theta$ (inscribed angles on 2-side arcs). So $C$ is the reflection of $B$ in $A_7A_8$ and $[A_7A_8B] = \frac12 s\cdot MC$.

So we must prove $2\,MD + MA_1 = 2\,MF + MC$.

**Step 3: two rhombi.** Let $E = A_5A_{12} \cap A_3A_{10}$ (on $\ell$). Inscribed angles give
$$\angle A_8A_5A_{10} = \angle A_7A_{10}A_5 = \angle A_{12}A_5A_{10} = \angle A_3A_{10}A_5 = 2\theta,$$
so triangles $A_5CA_{10}$ and $A_5EA_{10}$ are congruent isosceles triangles on opposite sides of $A_5A_{10}$, and $A_5CA_{10}E$ is a rhombus; its center $D$ is the midpoint of $CE$, so $2\,MD = MC + ME$. In the same way $\angle A_{10}A_3A_{12} = \angle A_5A_{12}A_3 = \angle A_1A_3A_{12} = \angle A_3A_{12}A_1 = 2\theta$, so $A_3EA_{12}A_1$ is a rhombus with center $F$, and $2\,MF = ME + MA_1$. Therefore
$$2\,MD + MA_1 = MC + ME + MA_1 = MC + 2\,MF.$$
This proves that the shaded area equals the unshaded area, i.e. half of the whole figure. ∎

(Numerically, for circumradius 1 the shaded area is $1.52538\ldots$, exactly half of the total $3.05076\ldots$)
